records.title: Harvesting finger millet
records.summary: Pick ripe heads in two rounds, because finger millet ripens unevenly.
instructions: Cut the brown heads first; return a week or so later to cut the rest.
Cut heads with a knife or by hand, leaving stalks standing for residue.
Dry heads before threshing by beating gently with a stick on a sheet.
limitations: Uneven ripening means some loss if you wait for every head.
ripeness_cues_see: Main heads turn brown and the 'fingers' look dry
Grain inside is brown to reddish and firm
ripeness_cues_feel: Grains feel hard and do not squash when pressed with a fingernail
method: Cut the brown heads first; return a week or so later to cut the rest.
Cut heads with a knife or by hand, leaving stalks standing for residue.
Dry heads before threshing by beating gently with a stick on a sheet.
drying_storage: Dry on a clean sheet or mat in the sun, off the bare soil, turning often; cover at night and if rain threatens.
Grain is dry enough when a grain bitten between the teeth cracks instead of squashing.
Store in clean, dry, tightly closed containers (sealed jars, tins or well-tied sacks inside containers), off the floor.
Check stored grain every week or two for insects, warmth or mould smell.
Raise stores off the ground on stones or a platform to keep out damp and rats; a few dry neem leaves in the container are a traditional extra.
do_not_store: Grain mixed with soil or stones
Grain from plants that showed heavy disease
residue_handling: Lay healthy stalks and leaves back on pits and beds as mulch, or add them to compost.
Remove and safely burn or bury far from the plot any residue with heavy disease or striga.

records.title: Harvesting pearl millet
records.summary: Cut heads when grains are hard and dry; guard ripening heads from birds.
instructions: Cut heads with a knife; leave stalks standing for residue.
Dry heads further, then thresh by beating on a clean sheet.
limitations: Birds can take much of the crop in the last weeks.
ripeness_cues_see: Heads turn from green to straw or grey-brown
A small dark spot shows at the base of grains
ripeness_cues_feel: Grain is hard and cannot be dented with a fingernail
Grains rub out of the head easily
method: Cut heads with a knife; leave stalks standing for residue.
Dry heads further, then thresh by beating on a clean sheet.
drying_storage: Dry on a clean sheet or mat in the sun, off the bare soil, turning often; cover at night and if rain threatens.

do_not_store: Grain mixed with soil or stones
Grain from plants that showed heavy disease
residue_handling: Lay healthy stalks and leaves back on pits and beds as mulch, or add them to compost.
Remove and safely burn or bury far from the plot any residue with heavy disease or striga.

records.title: Harvesting little millet
records.summary: Cut whole plants or heads when most grains are hard and the plants turn straw-coloured.
instructions: Cut plants near the base, bundle and dry, then thresh on a sheet.
limitations: Grain shatters if left too long.
method: Cut plants near the base, bundle and dry, then thresh on a sheet.
drying_storage: Dry on a clean sheet or mat in the sun, off the bare soil, turning often; cover at night and if rain threatens.
Grain is dry enough when a grain bitten between the teeth cracks instead of squashing.
Store in clean, dry, tightly closed containers (sealed jars, tins or well-tied sacks inside containers), off the floor.
Check stored grain every week or two for insects, warmth or mould smell.
Raise stores off the ground on stones or a platform to keep out damp and rats; a few dry neem leaves in the container are a traditional extra.
do_not_store: Grain mixed with soil or stones
Grain from plants that showed heavy disease
residue_handling: Lay healthy stalks and leaves back on pits and beds as mulch, or add them to compost.

records.title: Harvesting cowpea
records.summary: Pick dry pods repeatedly as they ripen; young green pods and leaves can be eaten earlier.
instructions: Pick dry pods by hand every few days.
Dry pods further in the sun, then beat them in a sack or on a sheet to release seeds.
limitations: Pods left too long can split and drop seed.
ripeness_cues_see: Pods turn from green to straw-coloured or brown
Pods look dry and slightly shrivelled
ripeness_cues_feel: Pods feel dry and papery and rattle when shaken
method: Pick dry pods by hand every few days.
Dry pods further in the sun, then beat them in a sack or on a sheet to release seeds.
drying_storage: Dry on a clean sheet or mat in the sun, off the bare soil, turning often; cover at night and if rain threatens.
Grain is dry enough when a grain bitten between the teeth cracks instead of squashing.
Store in clean, dry, tightly closed containers (sealed jars, tins or well-tied sacks inside containers), off the floor.
Check stored grain every week or two for insects, warmth or mould smell.
Raise stores off the ground on stones or a platform to keep out damp and rats; a few dry neem leaves in the container are a traditional extra.
residue_handling: Pull or cut plants at the base and leave the roots in the soil; lay stalks back as mulch.

records.title: Harvesting horse gram
records.summary: Harvest whole plants when most pods are dry and brown.
instructions: Cut or pull whole plants, dry them in the sun, then beat to thresh.
limitations: Pods shatter if left too long in the sun.
method: Cut or pull whole plants, dry them in the sun, then beat to thresh.
drying_storage: Dry on a clean sheet or mat in the sun, off the bare soil, turning often; cover at night and if rain threatens.
Grain is dry enough when a grain bitten between the teeth cracks instead of squashing.
Store in clean, dry, tightly closed containers (sealed jars, tins or well-tied sacks inside containers), off the floor.
Check stored grain every week or two for insects, warmth or mould smell.
Raise stores off the ground on stones or a platform to keep out damp and rats; a few dry neem leaves in the container are a traditional extra.
residue_handling: Leave roots in the soil; return stalks and leaves as mulch.

records.title: Harvesting niger
records.summary: Cut plants when flower heads turn brown and seeds turn dark.
instructions: Cut plants, stack heads-up to dry, then beat on a sheet to collect the small seeds.
limitations: Seeds shatter easily if left too long.
method: Cut plants, stack heads-up to dry, then beat on a sheet to collect the small seeds.
drying_storage: Dry on a clean sheet or mat in the sun, off the bare soil, turning often; cover at night and if rain threatens.
Grain is dry enough when a grain bitten between the teeth cracks instead of squashing.
Store in clean, dry, tightly closed containers (sealed jars, tins or well-tied sacks inside containers), off the floor.
Check stored grain every week or two for insects, warmth or mould smell.
Raise stores off the ground on stones or a platform to keep out damp and rats; a few dry neem leaves in the container are a traditional extra.
residue_handling: Lay healthy stalks and leaves back on pits and beds as mulch, or add them to compost.
Remove and safely burn or bury far from the plot any residue with heavy disease or striga.

records.title: Harvesting groundnut
records.summary: Lift plants when most pods are mature: inner shell darkened, kernels full.
instructions: Loosen the bed soil and pull plants by hand; shake off soil.
Dry plants with pods attached, pods upward, then pick pods off.
limitations: Pods left too long in dry ground can be lost or eaten by termites.
ripeness_cues_see: Inside of opened shells shows dark veining
method: Loosen the bed soil and pull plants by hand; shake off soil.
Dry plants with pods attached, pods upward, then pick pods off.
drying_storage: Dry pods thoroughly in the sun off the ground; store in pods in dry, aired sacks or containers.
do_not_store: Mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured nuts (moulds can be poisonous)
residue_handling: Return haulms (stalks and leaves) as mulch or compost.

records.title: Harvesting pigeon pea
records.summary: Pick dry pods in rounds as they ripen.
instructions: Pick or cut pod clusters; dry and beat to thresh.
limitations: Pod borers can damage many pods.
method: Pick or cut pod clusters; dry and beat to thresh.
drying_storage: Dry on a clean sheet or mat in the sun, off the bare soil, turning often; cover at night and if rain threatens.
Grain is dry enough when a grain bitten between the teeth cracks instead of squashing.
Store in clean, dry, tightly closed containers (sealed jars, tins or well-tied sacks inside containers), off the floor.
Check stored grain every week or two for insects, warmth or mould smell.
Raise stores off the ground on stones or a platform to keep out damp and rats; a few dry neem leaves in the container are a traditional extra.
residue_handling: Leave stems as stakes or fuel; leaves fall as mulch.

records.title: Harvesting cashew
records.summary: Collect nuts after the fruits fall naturally; dry them in the sun until the kernel rattles.
instructions: Collect fallen nuts often: at least weekly in dry weather, daily in wet weather, because they rot on the ground.
Twist the nut off the fruit by hand.
Sun-dry nuts for a few days on mats, turning them often.
limitations: First harvests come only after several years.
safety_notes: Never bite or crack raw nuts: the shell liquid burns skin and lips; roasting releases irritating smoke.
ripeness_cues_see: Fruit ('apple') coloured and fallen with the nut attached
ripeness_cues_feel: Dried nut is light and the kernel rattles inside when shaken
method: Collect fallen nuts often: at least weekly in dry weather, daily in wet weather, because they rot on the ground.
Twist the nut off the fruit by hand.
Sun-dry nuts for a few days on mats, turning them often.
drying_storage: Store dried raw nuts in dry bags or containers off the floor for processing.
Processed kernels keep best in airtight containers.
do_not_store: Nuts left on wet ground for days
residue_handling: Leave leaf litter under trees as mulch.

records.title: Harvesting mango
records.summary: Pick mature fruits carefully; let them ripen in the shade.
instructions: Pick by hand or with a pole and bag; leave a short stalk; avoid dropping fruit.
limitations: Years before fruiting.
safety_notes: Sap can burn skin; wipe and wash.
ripeness_cues_see: Skin colour starts to change near the stalk
method: Pick by hand or with a pole and bag; leave a short stalk; avoid dropping fruit.
drying_storage: Ripen in shade on a dry layer of leaves or straw; eat or dry slices soon after.
residue_handling: Return fallen leaves under the tree as mulch.

records.title: Lopping gliricidia for mulch
records.summary: Cut leafy branches a few times a season and lay them on beds and pits as mulch and green manure.
instructions: Cut leafy branches with a machete above knee height, leaving the main stems to resprout.
Lay leaves on beds; use straight stems as stakes.
limitations: Lopping too often weakens the hedge.
safety_notes: Seeds and bark are toxic; keep children away from them.
ripeness_cues_see: Branches leafy and longer than an arm
method: Cut leafy branches with a machete above knee height, leaving the main stems to resprout.
Lay leaves on beds; use straight stems as stakes.
drying_storage: Use leaves fresh as mulch; stems can be dried for fuel.
do_not_store: Do not store leaves as food.
residue_handling: All loppings go back onto the soil.

records.title: Picking amaranth greens
records.summary: Pick young leaves and tips often once plants are about a hand tall; regular picking keeps leaves coming.
instructions: Pinch or cut the youngest leaves and tips, leaving lower leaves to keep growing.
Pick every few days; pinch off flower heads unless saving seed.
Pull whole plants when thinning and eat them.
limitations: Leaves spoil within a day once picked.
safety_notes: Wash in clean water and cook before eating.
ripeness_cues_see: Plants about a hand tall with several soft leaves
Leaves bright and tender, before flower heads form
method: Pinch or cut the youngest leaves and tips, leaving lower leaves to keep growing.
Pick every few days; pinch off flower heads unless saving seed.
Pull whole plants when thinning and eat them.
drying_storage: Eat fresh the same day if possible.
To keep, spread leaves in a thin layer to dry in shade or light sun on a clean cloth, then store in a closed jar.
do_not_store: Leaves that are damp when stored (they mould)
residue_handling: Return old stalks to the pit as mulch; let a few plants flower and dry for seed.

records.title: Harvesting sorghum
records.summary: Cut heads when grains are hard and their colour is set; guard ripening heads from birds.
instructions: Cut heads with a knife, leaving stalks standing for residue.
Dry heads fully, then thresh by beating on a clean sheet.
limitations: Birds can take much of the crop near harvest.
ripeness_cues_feel: Grain hard and cannot be dented with a fingernail
method: Cut heads with a knife, leaving stalks standing for residue.
Dry heads fully, then thresh by beating on a clean sheet.
drying_storage: Dry on a clean sheet or mat in the sun, off the bare soil, turning often; cover at night and if rain threatens.
Grain is dry enough when a grain bitten between the teeth cracks instead of squashing.
Store in clean, dry, tightly closed containers (sealed jars, tins or well-tied sacks inside containers), off the floor.
Check stored grain every week or two for insects, warmth or mould smell.
Raise stores off the ground on stones or a platform to keep out damp and rats; a few dry neem leaves in the container are a traditional extra.
do_not_store: Grain mixed with soil or stones
Grain from plants that showed heavy disease
residue_handling: Lay healthy stalks and leaves back on pits and beds as mulch, or add them to compost.
Remove and safely burn or bury far from the plot any residue with heavy disease or striga.

records.title: Harvesting sweet potato
records.summary: Dig roots when vines yellow and growth slows; a test dig shows firm, full roots. Cure before storing.
instructions: Cut back vines first, then loosen the mound with a stick or hands and lift roots gently.
Do not bruise or cut roots; damaged roots rot in store.
Dig as needed: roots left a little longer in the mound keep, but weevils increase.
limitations: Roots keep only some weeks in a simple store.
safety_notes: Cook before eating; discard bitter, weevil-damaged parts.
ripeness_cues_see: Cracks in the mound over swelling roots
ripeness_cues_feel: A test root feels firm and full
Skin does not rub off easily
method: Cut back vines first, then loosen the mound with a stick or hands and lift roots gently.
Do not bruise or cut roots; damaged roots rot in store.
Dig as needed: roots left a little longer in the mound keep, but weevils increase.
drying_storage: Cure roots in shade for a few days so the skin toughens.
Store cool, dark and airy, raised off the floor; check often and eat damaged ones first.
Surplus can be sliced thinly and sun-dried.
do_not_store: Bruised, cut or weevil-tunnelled roots (eat first)
Roots with soft or rotting patches
residue_handling: Keep healthy vine tips in shade as cuttings for the next planting; lay the rest on beds as mulch.

records.title: Harvesting and safely processing cassava
records.summary: Roots can be dug from about eight months to a year on, as needed. Fresh roots spoil within days of digging and must always be processed and cooked thoroughly.
instructions: Dig carefully around one plant at a time and lift roots without breaking them.
Leave other plants in the ground until needed: the ground is the best store.
Cut healthy stems into pieces for replanting and keep them in shade.
limitations: Bitter cassava types need longer, more careful processing.
safety_notes: Never eat cassava raw: natural poisons are removed only by proper peeling, soaking and cooking.
ripeness_cues_see: Plant has stood through most of a year
ripeness_cues_feel: A test root is thick and firm
method: Dig carefully around one plant at a time and lift roots without breaking them.
Leave other plants in the ground until needed: the ground is the best store.
Cut healthy stems into pieces for replanting and keep them in shade.
drying_storage: Use fresh roots within a day or two of digging.
Peel, slice, soak and cook thoroughly following the locally known safe method; never eat raw.
Sun-dried slices of properly processed cassava keep longer in a dry, sealed container.
do_not_store: Fresh roots older than a couple of days (they spoil and turn streaky)
Roots with rot or a sour smell
residue_handling: Return leaves and peel to compost, not to animals unless local practice confirms it is safe.

records.title: Harvesting pineapple
records.summary: Pick when the fruit changes colour from the base and smells sweet.
instructions: Cut the fruit with a short stalk; keep the leafy top for replanting.
limitations: First fruit takes well over a year.
ripeness_cues_see: Skin colour turning from the base upward
method: Cut the fruit with a short stalk; keep the leafy top for replanting.
drying_storage: Eat fresh within days, or slice thinly and sun-dry on a clean surface.
residue_handling: Replant tops and side shoots (slips); lay old leaves as mulch.

records.title: Gathering neem leaves and seed
records.summary: Gather leaves lightly from established trees for pest washes and grain stores; collect fallen ripe seed for sowing.
instructions: Pick or cut a few leafy twigs at a time without stripping the tree.
Collect fallen ripe fruits, wash off the pulp and dry the seed in shade.
limitations: Young trees should not be stripped.
safety_notes: Neem products are not food; keep away from children.
ripeness_cues_see: Mature trees with plenty of leaves
method: Pick or cut a few leafy twigs at a time without stripping the tree.
Collect fallen ripe fruits, wash off the pulp and dry the seed in shade.
drying_storage: Dry leaves in shade and keep in a closed jar.
Sow seed soon: it loses life within a few months.
residue_handling: Leave leaf fall under the tree as mulch.

records.title: Picking moringa leaves and pods
records.summary: Pick young leaf sprigs often and tender pods while they still snap.
instructions: Strip young leaflets from sprigs; cut tender pods with a knife.
Prune the top after picking to keep the tree low.
limitations: Leaves are a supplement, not a staple.
safety_notes: Cook leaves and pods before eating.
ripeness_cues_see: Soft young leaf sprigs at branch tips
method: Strip young leaflets from sprigs; cut tender pods with a knife.
Prune the top after picking to keep the tree low.
drying_storage: Dry leaves in shade, crumble and keep in a closed jar.
Cook pods fresh.
residue_handling: Prunings go on beds as mulch.

records.title: Cutting sunn hemp for green manure
records.summary: Cut plants as the first flowers open and lay them on beds or mix them into pits.
instructions: Cut near the base with a machete or knife.
Lay the cut plants over beds as mulch or chop and mix them into pit fill.
limitations: Left too long, stems turn woody and rot slowly.
safety_notes: Seeds can be poisonous to people and animals.
ripeness_cues_feel: Stems still soft enough to cut easily
method: Cut near the base with a machete or knife.
Lay the cut plants over beds as mulch or chop and mix them into pit fill.
drying_storage: Not stored as food; leave one small patch to set seed for next time, and keep that seed away from food stores.
do_not_store: Never store seed with food grain
residue_handling: All cut material goes back onto the soil.

records.title: Trimming the grass hedge
records.summary: Trim the hedge once it is dense and lay the cut leaves as mulch.
instructions: Cut leaves back to about knee-high with a machete, leaving the clumps intact.
limitations: Trimming too often weakens the hedge.
safety_notes: Keep dry trimmings away from fire.
ripeness_cues_see: Hedge dense and taller than knee-high
method: Cut leaves back to about knee-high with a machete, leaving the clumps intact.
drying_storage: Use cut leaves as mulch straight away.
residue_handling: All trimmings go on beds and pits as mulch.
